t: Publish your first website with an AI agent
d: You'll end with your own version of a real website, live on the web, made by telling an AI agent what you want. Work from your phone or your computer.
s: You type or say what you want. The agent does the work. You check it. Most pages give you a Say this prompt to copy or dictate to the agent. You do things by hand only where the agent has no access: creating your GitHub account, signing in, approving a permission request, installing VS Code if you take that path, and changing a setting on github.com. The main one is turning on GitHub Pages, once, in your repo's Settings → Pages. Change the site title to "A History of St. Petersburg" and show me what you changed.

Your own site at https://your-username.github.io/your-repo/, on a subject you choose. You start by copying one of two real sites: history-of-tampa, one long scrolling story. Use it to learn any history subject: a city or neighborhood, a material like indigo, an industry, a company or a movement. Researching, sourcing and telling the story is how you learn it. startup-india-guide, a multi-page minisite with a sidebar, like this guide. Use it to organize any subject that needs several pages: a directory, a handbook, a resource guide or a program catalog. The running example turns history-of-tampa into a history of St. Petersburg, Florida, in a repo called history-of-st-pete. All four sites below are live. Starter · easiest · learn a history history-of-tampa 200 years of downtown Tampa as one scrolling story. Plain files, no build step. Same engine, new topic history-of-indigo The Tampa site's engine, telling the history of a dye instead of a city. Starter · harder · multi-page minisite startup-india-guide India's startup schemes as a searchable site with a sidebar. The agent runs its build step. Built from startup-india-guide Florida Startup Ecosystem Map A directory with a sidebar. Its repo is private, so you can look but not copy it.

Step 2 is the only fork in the road: the app path or the VS Code path. Both lead to the same published site. Step 1 · GitHub Create your GitHub account Free. Your username becomes part of your site's address. Step 2 · Set up your agent App or VS Code? The app path needs nothing installed. The VS Code path works on your computer. Step 3 · Just enough Git Repos, forks, commits and pushes The few words you need, and the prompts that do the work. Step 4 · Make it yours Pick a starter and rewrite it Copy history-of-tampa or startup-india-guide, then tell the agent your subject. Step 5 · Publish Turn on GitHub Pages One setting you switch on yourself. Then your site is live.

A GitHub account. It's free. Step 1 walks you through it. A paid AI plan. Claude Pro or higher for Claude Code, or ChatGPT Plus or higher for Codex. The free Claude plan doesn't include Claude Code. A phone or a computer. The app path works from a phone or a browser. The VS Code path needs a computer.

d: Your site lives in three places, and the agent works in only one of them. Once you see how they connect, the rest of the guide makes sense.
s: The agent edits the working copy. Its changes reach GitHub, and then your live site, only when it pushes. The working copy. The copy the agent actually edits. On the VS Code path it's a folder on your computer. On the app path it's a fresh copy in the cloud, made for each session. Nothing here reaches GitHub until it's pushed. Your repository on GitHub. The official copy of your site's files, plus the history of every saved change. It lives at github.com/your-username/your-repo. The live website. GitHub Pages builds it from your repository and serves it at https://your-username.github.io/your-repo/. Changes can take up to 10 minutes to show after a push. You switch Pages on yourself, once, in your repo's settings on github.com. The agent edits files, not your repo's settings, so this one is yours. Turn on GitHub Pages shows how. Four words move changes between them. You'll rarely type them yourself; you'll ask the agent. Word What it does Clone Makes a working copy of a repository. Pull Brings the working copy up to date with GitHub. Commit Saves a snapshot of your changes, with a short note. Push Sends your commits up to GitHub.
Type or say what you want in plain words, and name the repo it should work in.
It reads the files in the working copy and works out what to change. On a big job, ask to see the plan before it starts.
It edits files and runs commands in that working copy. It may stop and ask permission before a command or a risky step. Read the request before you approve it.
Look at what changed. When you're happy, tell it to save the work to GitHub: Commit and push to main. Once GitHub Pages is on, your live site updates too. Commit & push covers this step in detail.
What it can see, and what it remembers

Only what you give it. It works in the folder you opened in VS Code, or the repos you picked in the app. It doesn't see the rest of your computer unless you allow it. Don't count on it remembering. It doesn't carry your conversations into a new session. On your computer, Claude Code keeps a few short notes of its own, but what reliably carries over is the repo: its files, its history and a rules file. Claude reads CLAUDE.md at the start of every session, and Codex reads AGENTS.md. Put standing rules there, such as who to commit as or "never invent facts". Commit as yourself shows one. You can answer two questions: where does the agent make its edits (the working copy), and what makes them show up on your site (commit and push, then Pages publishes)?

t: How to talk to the agent
n: How to talk to the agent
d: Talk to the agent like a capable helper who can't see your screen: say what you want, where, and what done looks like. Then check its work.
s: Dictation is often faster than typing, and the agent doesn't need perfect sentences. Phone: tap the microphone on your keyboard and speak into the message box. Windows: click in the message box and press Win + H to start voice typing. Mac: turn on Dictation in System Settings → Keyboard. Then use the Dictation shortcut shown there, or Edit → Start Dictation. Read it back before you send. Dictation mishears names, repo names and email addresses.
The shape of a good prompt

Every good prompt answers three questions: What do you want? Where: which repo or folder? What does done look like? "Make it about St. Pete" is too vague. This works: In your-username/your-repo, change the site title to "A History of St. Petersburg" and rewrite the opening section about St. Petersburg, Florida. Cite a link for every fact you add. Done means the opening section is about St. Petersburg, not Tampa. If the session has more than one repo, add: "Work only in your-username/your-repo. Treat the other repos as read-only reference."

Before a change that touches many files, ask for a plan and approve it before any edits. Plan this first. Don't change anything until I say go. Claude Code also has a Plan mode that does the same thing.

After each change, ask for a summary you can actually read: Show me what you changed in plain English. Don't like it? Ask the agent to undo it. Undo that last change. Already committed and pushed? Git keeps every committed version, so you can still go back. Say "Revert the last commit and push to main."
Copy the whole error message, not a summary of it, and paste it back: Here's the error: paste the exact error. Explain what went wrong in plain English and fix it.

Never paste passwords, tokens or keys into a prompt or a file. Anyone can see a public repo, including its history. Read permission prompts before you approve. Pushes, deletes and installs deserve a look. If you're not sure, say no and ask the agent what the step does. Don't let it invent facts. A history site is only as good as its sources. Add this to any prompt that writes content: Only use facts you can cite with a link. Mark anything you can't verify as TBD. The Prompt cheat sheet collects the prompts you'll use most, ready to copy.

d: GitHub holds your site's files and publishes the site. Creating the account is one of the few steps no agent can do for you.
s: A free account is all you need. Once the agent is connected to your account, it does almost all the GitHub work. The main exception is turning on GitHub Pages in your repo's settings, which you'll click yourself in Step 5.

An agent can't create your account or change its settings: the account belongs to you and is tied to your email address. Do the GitHub steps in this guide in your phone's web browser, signed in at github.com. If you have the GitHub app on an iPhone, GitHub links open in that app instead. To open a link in Safari, long-press it and tap Open.
Go to https://github.com/signup and follow the prompts. You can also sign up with your Google or Apple account.

Your username becomes part of your site's address: https://your-username.github.io/. Keep it short and lowercase, since you'll share it in every link. Changing it later breaks old links, so pick one you'll keep.
GitHub asks you to verify your email address during sign-up. Do it right away. Until you do, you can't create or fork a repository, which this guide needs.

Recommended. It stops anyone who learns your password from getting in. Click your profile picture, then Settings → Password and authentication → Enable two-factor authentication. Use an authenticator app on your phone. Setting it up on the same phone as the app? You can't scan the QR code, so click setup key and type that code into the app instead. When GitHub shows your recovery codes, download them and keep them somewhere safe.
Keep your email private and copy your noreply address

Click your profile picture, then Settings → Emails. Tick Keep my email addresses private. GitHub then shows a private address that looks like this: ID+your-username@users.noreply.github.com Copy it. You'll give it to the agent so your commits are credited to you, without putting your real email in your site's public history. Commit as yourself shows how.
Save your details in this guide

Save your details here once; every prompt in this guide fills them in. Open https://github.com/your-username. You see your profile page. Your noreply address is copied somewhere you can find it again.

The username I want is taken Add a number or a hyphen, or try another spelling. Keep it lowercase. GitHub won't let me create or fork a repository Your email probably isn't verified yet. Open Settings → Emails and click Resend verification email under your address. Then click the link in the email GitHub sends. Check your spam folder if it doesn't arrive. Throwaway email addresses can't be verified, so use a real one.

d: You can run the agent in two places. The app path runs in a browser with nothing to install, or in the Claude app on your phone. The VS Code path runs on your computer. Pick one now; you can add the other later.
s: The app path The VS Code path What it is Claude Code in the Claude app VS Code with the Claude Code extension or the Codex extension Where the agent works On a fresh copy of your repo in the cloud In a folder on your computer What to install Nothing in a browser. On a phone, the Claude app. VS Code and the extension. The agent then installs Git and Node.js for you; the GitHub CLI is optional. On Windows, one setting to allow scripts. Devices A phone or tablet, any web browser, or the Claude desktop app A Mac or Windows computer What you do by hand Sign in, connect GitHub and install the Claude GitHub App, once. Turn on GitHub Pages in your repo's settings on github.com. Install VS Code and the extension, sign in, and approve the agent's requests. Turn on GitHub Pages on github.com, or let the GitHub CLI do it. Cost A paid Claude plan: Pro, Max, Team or an Enterprise seat that includes Claude Code For Claude Code, a paid Claude plan. For Codex, ChatGPT Plus or higher. Best for Beginners, phones, and the fastest start Seeing and opening your files on your computer, or using Codex Everything else, on both paths, you type or dictate to the agent. GitHub is free on both paths. The free Claude plan doesn't include Claude Code.

New to this, or on a phone? Start with the app path. It's the fastest way to a live site. Want to see the files on your computer? Pick the VS Code path. Codex users take this path too. Can't decide? You don't have to. Both paths work on the same repo, because the real copy lives on GitHub. Push from one, then pull in the other.

The app path · 2 pages Claude Code in the app Then: Many repos, one to work in. Then Step 3. The VS Code path · 3 or 4 pages VS Code + your agent Then: Git, Node & GitHub CLI; Windows: allow scripts (Windows only); Trusted folders. Then Step 3. This guide covers Codex on the VS Code path. OpenAI also runs Codex in the cloud at https://chatgpt.com/codex, but this guide doesn't cover that version.

d: Run Claude Code from a browser, the Claude app on your phone, or the Claude desktop app. Claude works on a fresh copy of your repo in the cloud, so you install no developer tools.
s: Browser: go to https://claude.ai/code. Phone or tablet: install the Claude app from the App Store or Google Play, open it and tap the Code tab. No Code tab? Your plan may not include Claude Code. Desktop app: open the Code tab in the Claude desktop app (https://claude.com/download) and choose Cloud instead of Local. All three show the same sessions: start on your laptop, check in from your phone.

These steps are sign-ins and permissions on your own accounts, so only you can approve them. Do them once at https://claude.ai/code in any web browser, even on your phone. The Claude apps then use the same setup.

Use a Claude account on a paid plan: Pro, Max, Team or an Enterprise seat that includes Claude Code. No account yet? Create one at https://claude.ai and upgrade to Pro. The free plan doesn't include Claude Code.
Claude asks you to connect GitHub and opens GitHub's authorization page. Approve it, and GitHub sends you back. On a Team or Enterprise plan, an admin may need to turn on GitHub access first.

Onboarding may offer it; if you skipped it, open https://github.com/apps/claude/installations/new. Choose your account. On a new account, choose All repositories and click Install. You don't have a repo of your own yet, and this way every repo you make in this guide works with Claude. Claude can read public repos without the app, but it needs the app to change your repos, public or private. Prefer to choose? Pick Only select repositories now, and add each repo after you make it (see "My repo isn't in the list" below).
The environment is the setup for Claude's cloud machine. Pro and Max get one named Default automatically. On Team or Enterprise, keep what's filled in on the form and click Create & finish.

Use the repository selector below the message box. Leave its branch selector on the default, usually main. No repo yet? Open https://claude.ai/code?repositories=fritzhand/history-of-tampa to start with the Tampa starter selected. You'll make your own copy in Step 3.
The mode menu next to the message box offers Auto (when available), Accept edits and Plan. Choose Plan to see the plan before anything changes.

Type it, or dictate it with the microphone on your keyboard: Explain what this repo is and how its website is built, in plain English. Don't change anything. Claude answers in plain English and changes no files. The session appears in the sidebar at claude.ai/code and in the Code tab of the Claude mobile app.

It works on a copy. Claude clones your repo into a fresh cloud machine and works on a new branch named claude/…. When it reaches a stopping point, it pushes that branch to GitHub. Each session starts fresh. Put standing rules in a CLAUDE.md file in your repo. Claude reads it at the start of every session. It commits as Claude unless you say otherwise. Commit as yourself shows the rule to add. It can't change your repo's settings. So you turn on GitHub Pages yourself, in Turn on GitHub Pages. You decide when the work reaches main, the branch your live site is built from. When you're happy, say: Commit and push to main. Or open the diff view, the panel that shows what Claude changed, select Create PR at the top, and merge the pull request on GitHub. The main branch explains both. What the agent runs for you The cloud machine clones your repo and puts the session on its own branch. Then Claude commits and pushes there: # the cloud machine, before Claude starts git clone https://github.com/your-username/your-repo.git git switch -c claude/task-name # Claude git add . git commit -m "Describe the change" git push -u origin claude/task-name When you say "Commit and push to main", it moves the work onto main and pushes that instead: git switch main git merge claude/task-name git push origin main

My repo isn't in the list If you chose Only select repositories, each new repo or fork needs adding. On GitHub, click your profile picture, then Settings → Applications → Installed GitHub Apps. Click Configure next to Claude, select the repo under Repository access, and click Save. Then start a new session and pick the repo. Claude says it can't push Install the Claude GitHub App on that repo (see above), then ask again. Claude also can't push to a repo that isn't yours, such as the original starter. Make your own copy first, in Clone, fork or copy.

t: Many repos, one to work in
n: Many repos, one to work in
d: Add several repos to one session so Claude can learn from them. Then name the one repo it may change.
s: The easiest way to get a site you like is to show Claude one. Add your own repo, plus a public repo to learn from: the starter you copied, such as fritzhand/history-of-tampa, or a site made from it, such as fritzhand/history-of-indigo. That's expected at this point. Read this page now, and use it once Clone, fork or copy has made your repo. Make your own version sends you back here. Claude can read every repo in the session. Your prompt names the one it may change.
Choose your own repo in the repository selector below the message box.
Add one or two more repos from the same selector. In the desktop app, click + next to the selected repository. Each repo shows its own branch selector; leave them on the default.
Name the one to work in

Claude puts all the repos side by side and starts in the folder above them, so it can't tell which one you mean. Always name it: Work only in your-username/your-repo. Treat the other repos as read-only reference. Ignore any CLAUDE.md in the reference repos. Look at how fritzhand/history-of-indigo turned the Tampa starter into the history of a topic, and tell me in plain English how to do the same for my subject. Don't change anything yet. Claude can read public repos, like both starters, without the Claude GitHub App. Your own repo, the one Claude pushes to, needs the app whether it's public or private. If you chose All repositories in Claude Code in the app, it's already covered. Ask "Which repo are you working in, and which files did you change?" Claude names your-username/your-repo, and every file it lists is in that repo. What the agent runs for you The session clones each repo into its own folder, side by side. Claude moves into your repo before it edits or commits anything: ls # history-of-indigo history-of-tampa your-repo cd your-repo

Claude changed files in the wrong repo Your starter on GitHub is safe: Claude can't push to a repo that isn't yours. Undo the stray edits and restate the rule: Undo your changes in fritzhand/history-of-tampa. Work only in your-username/your-repo. Treat the other repos as read-only reference.

d: Install VS Code, open a folder for your projects and add the Claude Code or Codex extension. These are the only installs you do by hand. After this page, you ask the agent.
s: The agent runs inside VS Code, so it can't install VS Code or itself. Trusting your folder and signing in are yours to do, too.

Download it from https://code.visualstudio.com. It's free. Open the downloaded .dmg file and drag Visual Studio Code into the Applications folder. Then open it from Applications. Run the installer you downloaded. It's the User Setup, which doesn't need admin rights. Keep the defaults and click through to the end.
Open a folder for your projects

In VS Code, choose File → Open Folder…. Go to your Documents folder and use the window's new-folder button to make a folder called Projects. Select it and open it. Each site you make will get its own folder inside Projects. VS Code opens a new folder in Restricted Mode, and a banner across the top says so. Click Manage in the banner, then click Trust. If a box asks Do you trust the authors of the files in this folder? instead, click Yes, I trust the authors. You made this folder, so it's safe. Until you trust it, VS Code turns off or limits AI agents. Trusted folders explains why.

You need a paid Claude plan: Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise. Open the Extensions view: Ctrl + Shift + X on Windows, Cmd + Shift + X on Mac. Search for Claude Code. Pick the one published by Anthropic and click Install. Click the Spark icon in the Activity Bar, the strip of icons down the left edge. It opens your list of Claude sessions. Start a new one there. Or open the Command Palette (Ctrl + Shift + P, or Cmd + Shift + P on Mac) and run Claude Code: Open in New Tab. The first time, a sign-in screen appears. Click Sign in and approve in the browser window that opens. You need ChatGPT Plus or higher. Open the Extensions view: Ctrl + Shift + X on Windows, Cmd + Shift + X on Mac. Search for Codex. Pick Codex – OpenAI's coding agent, published by OpenAI, and click Install. Click the Codex icon to open it. Don't see it? Open the Command Palette (Ctrl + Shift + P, or Cmd + Shift + P on Mac) and run Codex: Open Codex Sidebar. Choose Sign in with ChatGPT and finish in the browser. You don't need Node.js or anything else to run either extension.

In the agent's panel, start a new conversation. Type this into the message box, or dictate it: Check which of these are installed on this computer: git, node, and the GitHub CLI (gh). Tell me what's missing, in plain English. The agent may ask permission to run a command. Read it, then allow it. These checks only look up version numbers. The agent answers in plain English with what's installed and what's missing. Keep that answer for the next page, Git, Node & GitHub CLI, where the agent installs the missing tools.

I can't find the Spark icon Look in the Activity Bar down the left edge. It also appears at the top right of the editor, but only while a file is open. Still missing? A Restricted Mode banner at the top means VS Code doesn't trust the folder, so the extension is switched off and its icon is hidden. Click Manage in the banner, then Trust, or run Workspaces: Manage Workspace Trust from the Command Palette. Otherwise, run Developer: Reload Window from the Command Palette. On my Mac, a window offers to install developer tools A fresh Mac may offer this when something asks for Git. It's Apple's Command Line Tools, which include Git. Click Install, wait for it to finish, then carry on. Sign-in fails, or says my plan doesn't include it Claude Code needs Claude Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise. The free Claude plan doesn't include it. Codex needs ChatGPT Plus or higher. Check your plan, then sign in again. What the agent runs for you To answer your first prompt, the agent asks each tool for its version. A "not found" or "not recognized" error means the tool is missing. git --version node -v gh --version

d: Three free tools let the agent save versions of your site, build it, and handle GitHub for you. You ask, and the agent installs them.
s: Tool What it does for you Do you need it? Git Saves versions of your files and sends them to GitHub. Yes. Node.js Runs the build script some starters use: startup-india-guide, the multi-page starter, builds with node build.mjs. history-of-tampa, the one-page story, needs no build. Install it anyway. It's quick. GitHub CLI (gh) Lets the agent create and fork repos for you, and handles Git's sign-in to GitHub so pushes work. It can also turn on GitHub Pages, a shortcut for the setting you'd otherwise click on GitHub. Optional, but recommended. Without it, you create and fork repos yourself on github.com.

Install whatever is missing from git, node and the GitHub CLI (gh). Use the right method for this computer: winget on Windows; on a Mac, Homebrew if I have it, or xcode-select --install for git. If a step needs my password or a click in an installer window, stop and tell me exactly what to do.

The agent may ask before each install. Read the command, then allow it. Windows may ask whether to allow changes to your device, and a Mac may ask for your password. Both are normal for an install. If an installer window opens, keep the defaults.
Close every VS Code window, then open VS Code again. It only finds new tools when it starts.
Sign the GitHub CLI in to your account

This sign-in asks you questions and opens your browser, so you answer it, not the agent. Open the terminal with View → Terminal. Type this and press Enter: gh auth login Answer with the arrow keys and Enter. Choose GitHub.com, then HTTPS. Say yes when it offers to use your GitHub login for Git. Choose to log in with a web browser. It shows a one-time code. Note it, press Enter to open GitHub in your browser, enter the code there and authorize. Not sure what to pick? Ask the agent to walk you through it: Walk me through signing in to the GitHub CLI with gh auth login, one question at a time.

Set git's default branch for new repos to main. Then show me the versions of git, node and gh, and confirm gh is logged in. The agent shows a version number for git, node and gh, and says gh is logged in to github.com as your-username. If you or the agent see an error that includes running scripts is disabled on this system, go to Windows: allow scripts. It's a one-line fix. Then come back.
If the agent can't install them

Download each missing tool, run its installer and keep the defaults. Then restart VS Code. Git: open the terminal (View → Terminal), run xcode-select --install, and click Install in the window that appears. Node.js: go to https://nodejs.org, download the version labeled LTS as the macOS Installer (.pkg), and run it. GitHub CLI: install Homebrew by following https://brew.sh, then run brew install gh in the terminal. Git: download Git for Windows from https://git-scm.com/install/windows. On the page about the initial branch name, choose Override the default branch name for new repositories and type main. Node.js: go to https://nodejs.org, download the version labeled LTS as the Windows Installer (.msi), and run it. GitHub CLI: download the installer from https://cli.github.com and run it.

It says git, node or gh is "not recognized" or "not found", but I just installed it VS Code is still using the old settings from before the install. Close every VS Code window and open it again. On Windows, if that doesn't help, restart the computer. What the agent runs for you The exact commands depend on your computer. They look like this: # Windows (the --accept flags answer winget's yes/no questions, # which the agent can't type) winget install --id Git.Git -e --source winget --accept-source-agreements --accept-package-agreements winget install --id OpenJS.NodeJS.LTS -e --source winget --accept-source-agreements --accept-package-agreements winget install --id GitHub.cli -e --source winget --accept-source-agreements --accept-package-agreements # Mac xcode-select --install brew install node brew install gh # After the restart: new repos start on main, then the check git config --global init.defaultBranch main git --version node -v gh --version gh auth status

d: Windows blocks PowerShell scripts until you allow them, and Node's tools need them. One setting fixes it for your account. On a Mac? Skip this page.
s: You or the agent run npm, Node's tool installer, in the VS Code terminal, and get an error like this: npm : File C:\Program Files\nodejs\npm.ps1 cannot be loaded because running scripts is disabled on this system. The file named can also be codex.ps1 or claude.ps1. It's the same problem. Why: on Windows, VS Code's terminal runs Windows PowerShell. Its starting policy, called Restricted, runs single commands but no scripts. npm and the tools it installs start through small .ps1 script files, so PowerShell refuses them.

Allow PowerShell scripts for my user account only using Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser -Force, then check it with Get-ExecutionPolicy -List. Read the command in the permission prompt, then allow it. It doesn't need admin rights, and it works right away. -Force only skips PowerShell's "are you sure?" question, which the agent can't answer. Open the terminal with View → Terminal, paste this and press Enter. If PowerShell asks you to confirm, type Y and press Enter. Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser In the list from Get-ExecutionPolicy -List, the CurrentUser line says RemoteSigned. Run the command that failed again. It works now.

Scripts on your computer can run. Scripts downloaded from the internet still need a signature from a trusted publisher. It applies only to your Windows account. That's why it doesn't need admin rights. It stays set until you change it. Microsoft explains the settings in about_Execution_Policies.

It says my setting is overridden by a policy, or nothing changed On a work or school laptop, your IT department may set this policy for you, and theirs wins. Ask IT to allow it. Don't try to get around it. What the agent runs for you Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser -Force # -Force skips the Y/N question Get-ExecutionPolicy -List The list looks something like this. The line that matters is CurrentUser: Scope ExecutionPolicy ----- --------------- MachinePolicy Undefined UserPolicy Undefined Process Undefined CurrentUser RemoteSigned LocalMachine Undefined

t: Trusted folders: how the agent works in your folder
d: The folder you open is the agent's workspace. Trust only folders you made or got from people you trust, and read what the agent asks before you approve it.
s: The first time you open a folder, you trust it twice: once for VS Code, and sometimes once for the agent.

A folder you haven't trusted opens in Restricted Mode. A banner across the top says so, and AI agents and the terminal are turned off. The Claude Code extension doesn't work there. Click Manage in the banner, then Trust. Some setups ask up front instead: Do you trust the authors of the files in this folder? Yes, I trust the authors trusts it. No, I don't trust the authors keeps Restricted Mode.

The first time it works in a folder, the agent may ask its own version, such as whether you trust the files in this folder. The same rule applies. Trust a folder only if you made it or cloned it from someone you trust. Open the project folder itself, or your Projects folder, never your whole Documents or home folder. Trusting a folder also trusts every folder inside it.
How the agent works in your folder

The folder you open is the agent's workspace. It may still read files elsewhere on your computer, and it checks or asks before changing anything outside the folder. When the agent needs your OK to run a command, it shows a permission prompt. Read the command before you approve it. Pushes, deletes and installs deserve a careful look. To see a plan before any change, add this to your request: Plan this first. Don't change anything until I say go.
Which folder are you working in? List what's in it, and don't change anything. The agent names the folder you opened and lists its files. VS Code shows no Restricted Mode banner.

VS Code says Restricted Mode, and the agent doesn't work Click Manage in the Restricted Mode banner, then Trust. Or open the Command Palette (Ctrl + Shift + P, or Cmd + Shift + P on Mac), run Workspaces: Manage Workspace Trust and trust the folder. The agent asks about a folder I didn't expect Say no. Then check that VS Code opened your project folder, not a folder above it. The folder's name shows at the top of the Explorer view. Use File → Open Folder… to open the right one.

d: A repo (repository) is your project's folder on GitHub, plus the full history of every saved change. Your site gets one repo. Decide who can see it before you put anything in it.
s: A fork makes your repo for you, and a fork is what this guide recommends for a first site. Read "Public or private" and "Pick a name", then go on to Clone, fork or copy. Create a new repo here only when that page's "Make a fresh copy" steps send you back.

Public Private Who can see it Anyone on the internet, including every past version of every file Only you and people you invite GitHub Pages on a free account Yes No. It needs a paid GitHub plan, and the site itself is public anyway. Pick it for A website you're publishing, like the one in this guide Notes or work you don't want strangers to read For this guide, choose public. Git keeps every version. If you push a password, a key or someone's private details to a public repo, deleting the file later doesn't remove it: it's still in the history for anyone to find. Never put them in a repo.
Use lowercase with hyphens, such as history-of-st-pete. The name becomes part of your site's address, https://your-username.github.io/your-repo/, and web addresses are case-sensitive.
Create a new repo (fresh copy only)

Cloud sessions can only work in a repo that already exists, so this click is yours. Go to https://github.com/new. Type the name. Choose Public. Turn on the option to add a README. Click Create repository.
Open it in a new session

Start a new session and pick your-username/your-repo in the repository selector below the message box. If it isn't in the list, add it to the Claude GitHub App, as shown in Claude Code in the app. Open your Projects folder in VS Code. The agent creates the repo with the GitHub CLI you signed in to in Git, Node & GitHub CLI. Create a new public GitHub repository called your-repo with a README and clone it here. Then open it yourself: File → Open Folder…, choose Projects/your-repo, and start a new conversation there. Now the agent works in your repo and reads its CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md when it starts. Go to https://github.com/new, type the name, choose Public, turn on the option to add a README and click Create repository. Then say "Clone https://github.com/your-username/your-repo into this folder." and open it as above. If you created a repo, open https://github.com/your-username/your-repo. You see your repo's page with a README file and a Public label next to its name.

I made it private by mistake Visibility is a repo setting, so you change it on GitHub: open the repo's Settings, scroll to the Danger Zone section and click Change visibility. On the VS Code path, the agent can do it with the GitHub CLI: Make your-username/your-repo public. I pushed a password or key to a public repo Deleting the file isn't enough, because the history keeps it. Change the password, or cancel the key and make a new one, on the site that issued it. Do that first. Then ask the agent to remove the file. What the agent runs for you On the VS Code path, with the GitHub CLI: gh repo create your-repo --public --add-readme --clone # Make a private repo public gh repo edit your-username/your-repo --visibility public --accept-visibility-change-consequences

d: To make your own version of a starter, you fork it or copy it into a repo of your own. Cloning is how the agent gets a working copy of that repo to edit.
s: Fork: your own copy of someone else's repo, on GitHub. It stays linked to the original. Fresh copy: a brand-new repo of yours with the starter's files copied in. No link back, and its history starts fresh. Clone: a working copy of a repo, on your computer or in the cloud. It stays linked to the repo it came from, so the agent can push its changes back. Fork or copy the starter once to get a repo of your own. The agent then works in a clone of that repo.

Good Watch out Fork Fastest: one prompt with the GitHub CLI, or two clicks on GitHub. A fork of a public repo is always public; you can't make it private. Commits in a fork don't count on your GitHub profile. Fresh copy How the real examples were made: history-of-indigo from history-of-tampa, and the Florida ecosystem map from startup-india-guide. You choose public or private, and your commits count on your profile. A few more steps, which the agent does for you. A fork is fine for a first site. Make a fresh copy if you want your work to show on your GitHub profile. The steps below use fritzhand/history-of-tampa, one long scrolling story that works for any history subject. For a multi-page site with a sidebar, on any subject, swap in fritzhand/startup-india-guide. Pick a starter compares them.
Do this once. If you fork here, skip "Get your copy" in Make your own version.

Cloud sessions work only with repos that already exist, so this click is yours. Open https://github.com/fritzhand/history-of-tampa and click Fork in the top-right corner. Type your-repo as the repository name, leave the other options as they are, and click Create fork.

Start a new session and pick your fork in the repository selector. If it isn't in the list, add it to the Claude GitHub App, as shown in Claude Code in the app. Open your Projects folder in VS Code, then say: Fork fritzhand/history-of-tampa into my account and name the fork your-repo. Then clone it here. Then open it yourself: File → Open Folder…, choose Projects/your-repo, and start a new conversation there. Now the agent works in your repo and reads its CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md when it starts. Open https://github.com/fritzhand/history-of-tampa, click Fork, type your-repo as the repository name and click Create fork. Then say "Clone https://github.com/your-username/your-repo into this folder." and open it as above.
Follow "Create a new repo" in Repos: public or private. The starter's files will replace its README.
Start a session with both repos
Select your repo and fritzhand/history-of-tampa, as shown in Many repos, one to work in.

Work only in your-username/your-repo. Treat the other repos as read-only reference. Copy every file from fritzhand/history-of-tampa into my repo (not the .git folder), commit and push to main. Open your Projects folder in VS Code, then say: Create a new public GitHub repository called your-repo and clone it here. Copy every file from https://github.com/fritzhand/history-of-tampa into it (not the .git folder), commit and push to main. Then open it yourself: File → Open Folder…, choose Projects/your-repo, and start a new conversation there. Now the agent works in your repo and reads its CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md when it starts.

The steps above already give the agent a clone: on the app path, each session clones the repos you pick, and on the VS Code path, the prompts clone into Projects. To get your repo onto another computer, open that computer's Projects folder in VS Code and say: Clone https://github.com/your-username/your-repo into this folder. Then open Projects/your-repo as above. Clone your own repo, not the original: the agent can't push to a repo that isn't yours. Open https://github.com/your-username/your-repo. It shows the starter's files. A fork also says "forked from fritzhand/history-of-tampa" under its name.

The agent says it can't push It's probably working in the original starter, which isn't yours. Tell it which repo to use: Work only in your-username/your-repo. Treat the other repos as read-only reference. On the app path, also check that the Claude GitHub App is installed on your repo. See Claude Code in the app. GitHub says the name is already taken You already have a repo with that name, maybe from an earlier fork. Use that repo, or pick a new name. I forked, but I want my commits to count Make a fresh copy under a new name, as above, and use that one from now on. You can delete the fork later. What the agent runs for you # Fork, and clone the fork (GitHub CLI) gh repo fork fritzhand/history-of-tampa --clone --fork-name your-repo # Fresh copy: make your repo, clone the starter next to it, # then copy the starter's files without its .git folder gh repo create your-repo --public --clone git clone https://github.com/fritzhand/history-of-tampa git -C history-of-tampa archive HEAD | tar -x -C your-repo cd your-repo git add . git commit -m "Copy the history-of-tampa starter" git push origin main # Clone git clone https://github.com/your-username/your-repo.git

d: A commit is a save point with a short note. A push sends your save points to GitHub, and that's what updates your live site.
s: Commit: a save point for the whole project, with a note that says what changed. You can go back to any commit. Push: sends your commits to GitHub. Until then, they exist only in the working copy. Pull: brings down changes made somewhere else, such as on GitHub's website or from your other device. Saving a file is not a commit. The agent saves files as it works, but nothing is in the history until it commits, and nothing is on GitHub until it pushes. Commits stay in the working copy until a push sends them to GitHub. Once GitHub Pages is on, a push to main rebuilds your site.

Commit and push to main. The agent writes a short note for the commit that says what changed. The agent may ask before it pushes. Check the repo and branch it names: your-username/your-repo, and main or, on the app path, Claude's own claude/… branch. The main branch explains the difference.

See what's been saved: Show me the last 5 commits in plain English. Undo a commit you already pushed. A revert adds a new commit that reverses the old one, so the record stays: Revert the last commit and push to main. Changed something on GitHub's website, or on your other device? Start with: Pull the latest changes from GitHub first. Open https://github.com/your-username/your-repo/commits/main. Your newest commit is at the top, with the message the agent wrote. Once Pages is on, your site shows the change within about 10 minutes.

The push was rejected because GitHub has changes I don't have Someone, maybe you on another device, pushed first. Bring those changes down, then push again: Pull first, then push again. Don't force-push. A force-push would overwrite the changes on GitHub. The agent committed, but my site didn't change The commit may not be pushed yet, or it went to a branch other than main. Ask: Is my last commit pushed to main on GitHub? If not, push it to main. It says there's a merge conflict Two changes touched the same lines. Let the agent explain it before anything is overwritten: Explain the conflict in plain English and suggest which version to keep. Don't change anything until I choose. What the agent runs for you git status # what changed since the last commit git add . git commit -m "Add St. Pete timeline" git push origin main git log --oneline -5 # the last 5 commits git revert --no-edit HEAD # a new commit that undoes the last one (add -m 1 for a merge) git pull --rebase # bring down GitHub's changes, then put yours on top

d: Your live site is published from one branch, main. Your changes reach the site only when they reach main.
s: A branch is a parallel line of work in the same repo. You can make changes on a branch without touching the main line. main is the line GitHub Pages publishes from, so your site updates only when main changes.

Repos you create on GitHub, and forks of the starters, already use main. On the VS Code path, Git, Node & GitHub CLI set your computer to use main for new repos too. If you ever have the agent start a repo from scratch, name the folder and the branch: In the your-repo folder, start a new git repository on a branch named main.
The app path: Claude's own branch

In the Claude app, Claude works on its own branch, named claude/…, and pushes that branch, not main. Your site doesn't change until the work is merged into main. Claude's commits wait on its own branch. Merging them into main is what updates your site.
Two ways to get work onto main
The simplest way for a project only you work on. Say it with the task, or at the start of the session: Commit and push to main.

Let Claude push its claude/… branch, then say: Open a pull request from your branch into main of your-username/your-repo (my repo, not the original) and merge it. Or tap Create PR at the top of the diff view. Then open the pull request on GitHub, click Merge pull request, then Confirm merge. GitHub may aim a pull request from a fork at the original repo. Before you merge, check that it goes into your-username/your-repo, not fritzhand/…. If it doesn't, close it and use the prompt above. On the VS Code path the agent usually works on main already, so "Commit and push to main." is all you need. Open https://github.com/your-username/your-repo/commits/main. Your change is the newest commit on main.

The agent says it can't push to main Use the pull request way instead: Push your branch, then open a pull request from it into main of your-username/your-repo (my repo, not the original) and merge it. The agent pushed, but my site didn't change The work is probably still on a claude/… branch. Ask: Which branch is my work on? Get it onto main and push main. After main changes, give GitHub Pages up to 10 minutes. What the agent runs for you # A new repo that starts on main git init -b main git config --global init.defaultBranch main # every new repo from now on # Pull request, then merge (GitHub CLI). Naming the repo keeps a fork's # pull request out of the original repo. gh pr create --repo your-username/your-repo --base main --fill gh pr merge branch-name --repo your-username/your-repo --merge On the app path, Claude may use its built-in GitHub tools for the pull request instead.

d: Every commit records an author. Give the agent your name and your GitHub noreply email so the work is credited to you, not to Claude.
s: In the Claude app, Claude's cloud machine commits as Claude <noreply@anthropic.com> unless you say otherwise. Those commits aren't credited to you and don't show on your GitHub profile. One sentence fixes it. Same work, same message. Only the author changes, and with it, who gets the credit.

It looks like ID+your-username@users.noreply.github.com. You copied it in Create your GitHub account. It's on GitHub under Settings → Emails. It credits you without putting your real email in your site's public history.

In your-username/your-repo, set git user.name to "Your Name" and user.email to "your-noreply-email", and commit as me from now on. Add this rule to a CLAUDE.md file at the root of that repo (create it if needed) so every session follows it: Commit as Your Name <your-noreply-email>. Before your first commit in each session, set git user.name and user.email to these in this repo. Then commit and push to main. Each session starts on a fresh machine, so the setting is gone next time. Claude reads CLAUDE.md at the start of every session, so the rule brings it back. The agent commits with your computer's git identity. Set it once, and it applies to every repo on this computer: Set my global git name to "Your Name" and email to "your-noreply-email". The name is what your commits show, usually your full name. It doesn't have to match your GitHub username. Open https://github.com/your-username/your-repo/commits/main. Your newest commit shows your name and profile picture as the author. Claude's picture may appear beside yours as a co-author, because Claude adds a Co-Authored-By line to the commit message. That's expected. Commits on main can take up to 24 hours to appear on your profile's contribution graph. Commits in a fork don't count there; see Clone, fork or copy.

My older commits still say Claude The setting changes only new commits. Leave the old ones as they are. My name shows on the commit, but not on my profile Check three things: the email is your noreply address exactly, the repo isn't a fork, and the commit is on main. Then allow up to 24 hours. What the agent runs for you # App path: this repo only (the machine is fresh each session) git config user.name "Your Name" git config user.email "your-noreply-email" # VS Code path: every repo on your computer git config --global user.name "Your Name" git config --global user.email "your-noreply-email" # Who wrote the last commit? git log -1 --format="%an <%ae>"

d: Don't start from a blank page. Copy a real, working site and have the agent rewrite it for your subject. One starter tells a history as a long scrolling story. The other organizes any subject into a multi-page guide with a sidebar.
s: Starter · learn a history · easiest history-of-tampa One long scrolling story of 200 years of downtown Tampa, with a map, charts and archival photos. Use it to learn any history by researching, sourcing and telling it: a city or neighborhood, a material like indigo, an industry, a company or a movement. Plain files, no build step. Starter · build a minisite · harder startup-india-guide A multi-page minisite with a sidebar and search, built from data files. Use it to organize any subject that needs several pages: a directory, a handbook, a resource guide or a program catalog. history-of-tampa startup-india-guide Build step? No Yes: node build.mjs, run by the agent Pages folder / (root) /docs Good for Learning any history: a place, an industry, a company, a movement Organizing any subject into pages: a directory, handbook, resource guide or program catalog Extra setup None (its optional data check uses Node) Node, on the VS Code path only Repo On GitHub On GitHub First time? Pick history-of-tampa. This guide's running example turns it into a history of St. Petersburg, Florida, but the same steps work for any history subject. Building a directory or guide instead? Pick startup-india-guide.

From history-of-tampa Indigo: The Blue That Dyed the World The same engine, pointed at a topic instead of a place: the history of a dye, on a world map. From startup-india-guide · showcase only Florida Startup Ecosystem Map A source-linked map of Florida's startup ecosystem. Its repo is private, so you can look but not fork it. Want a sidebar guide like the one you're reading? This guide is built the same way as startup-india-guide and published from main, /docs. Its repo is fritzhand/quickstart.

Have the agent walk you through a starter before you copy it. On the app path, add the starter to a session as a reference repo (Many repos, one to work in). Look at fritzhand/history-of-tampa and tell me, in plain English, which files I'd change to make a history of my subject, and what I should delete first. For the other starter, swap in fritzhand/startup-india-guide and "a guide to" instead of "a history of".
You may reuse both starters. Each comes with a few conditions.

Code: CC0. Free to reuse for anything, no credit required. Compiled data in js/data.js: CC BY 4.0. Reuse it only with credit. You'll replace it with your own research anyway. Author photo (assets/jeremy.jpg): all rights reserved. Delete it. Images the site shows: each carries its own license, listed in CONTENT_LICENSE.md. Keep the credit line for any image you keep.

Code: MIT. Free to reuse and change, but keep the LICENSE file with its copyright notice. Author photo (site/jeremy.png): a photo of the original author. Delete it. Keep a line such as "Forked from fritzhand/history-of-tampa", with a link, in your site's footer and README. It's a courtesy for the code, and it's how you credit any data or images you keep. You know which starter you'll use and which Pages folder it publishes from: / (root) for history-of-tampa, /docs for startup-india-guide. Next: Make your own version.

d: Turn a starter into a site about your own subject, one prompt at a time. The main example turns the Tampa history into a history of St. Petersburg, Florida, in a repo called history-of-st-pete. A second example builds a minisite with a sidebar.
s: Do the steps in order. Read what the agent says back after each one before you send the next. Your history doesn't have to be a city. The same steps work for a neighborhood, an industry, a company, a movement or a topic like indigo: wherever a prompt says St. Petersburg, Florida, put your subject. Researching and sourcing it is how you learn it. Building a multi-page guide instead, such as a directory, handbook or resource guide? Follow the second example.

Already forked or copied the starter in Clone, fork or copy? Skip to step 2. If not, fork it now. On the app path, send this in a session that has fritzhand/history-of-tampa selected. Fork fritzhand/history-of-tampa into my account, with only the main branch, and name the fork your-repo. If you can't choose the fork's name, stop and tell me. Don't fork it under another name. Open https://github.com/fritzhand/history-of-tampa and click Fork in the top-right corner. Type your-repo as the repository name, in lowercase, and click Create fork. Already forked under the wrong name? On your fork, click Settings, type the new name in Repository name and click Rename. Want your commits to count on your GitHub profile? Make a fresh copy instead, with a session that holds both repos. Clone, fork or copy shows how.
Start a session in your repo and set the rules

Start a new session and pick your-username/your-repo in the repository selector. Optional: add fritzhand/history-of-tampa as a read-only reference, as shown in Many repos, one to work in. Fork not in the list? Add it to the Claude GitHub App, as shown in Claude Code in the app. Open your projects folder in VS Code, then say: Clone https://github.com/your-username/your-repo into this folder and open it. Then send the rules as your first message: Work only in your-username/your-repo. Treat the other repos as read-only reference. Commit as Your Name <your-noreply-email>. Push finished work straight to main. Only use facts you can cite with a link, and mark anything you can't verify as TBD. Write these rules into a CLAUDE.md file at the root of my repo so every session follows them. Then commit and push to main. Using Codex? Say AGENTS.md instead of CLAUDE.md.
Clean out the original owner's things

The starter still carries its author's analytics tag, photo, name, links and planning notes. Left in, the tag would send your visitors' data to the original author. In index.html, remove the Google Analytics tag. Delete assets/jeremy.jpg and the author photo and name blocks in the byline, the About section and the credit footer. Delete the files I won't use: ybor.html, js/ybor-data.js, the assets/linkedin and assets/linkedin-ybor folders, and the LinkedIn tools in tools/. Delete the planning files ARCHIVAL_RESEARCH_PROMPT.md, ARCHIVAL_RESEARCH_PROMPT_TAMPA.md and DOWNTOWN_TAMPA_PLAN.md, and replace PROGRESS.md with a fresh one for my project. Remove any links to the deleted pages. Replace every https://fritzhand.github.io/history-of-tampa/ address with https://your-username.github.io/your-repo/ and point the Repository links to my repo. Then list what you removed, and commit and push to main.

Get the facts before the agent writes a word of your site. That keeps invented numbers out. Research the history of St. Petersburg, Florida, for this site. Use real sources, such as archives, libraries, universities, government records and newspapers, and give a working link for every fact, date and number. Wikipedia can point you to sources but isn't one. List images only if they're public domain or openly licensed, with a credit line. Write everything to research/notes.md and mark anything you couldn't verify as TBD. Never invent a number, date or link. Don't change the site yet. Ask "Show me research/notes.md" and read it. You know your subject: tell the agent to delete anything that looks wrong. On the app path, the cloud machine may block most websites. Paste the same research prompt into a regular Claude chat with web search on. Then bring the answer back to your session: Put these research results in research/notes.md exactly as written, then commit and push to main: paste the results

This is the biggest edit, so ask for a plan first: add "Plan this first. Don't change anything until I say go." Using only the facts in research/notes.md, rewrite js/data.js, the text in index.html and any Tampa labels in js/app.js for St. Petersburg, Florida. Keep the data file's format and the variable name tampaData so the site still works. Remove any section I have no data for instead of leaving it empty. Keep a line in the footer that says "Forked from fritzhand/history-of-tampa" with a link to it. Then show me what you changed in plain English.

Search the whole repo, ignoring capitals, for leftover words from the original: Tampa, Ybor and fritzhand. Don't rename code names such as tampaData, or file names the code loads. Keep mentions that belong in my history, such as Tampa Bay, and the "Forked from fritzhand/history-of-tampa" credit. Delete planning files that are only about Tampa, and fix every other word a visitor or reader would see, including README.md and js/app.js. Run node tools/validate-data.mjs and fix what it reports. Then summarize what changed in plain English.
Commit and push to main, then publish

Commit and push to main. Now switch on your site: Turn on GitHub Pages, from main and / (root). Each session starts fresh. End every session with: Update PROGRESS.md with what's done and what's next, then commit and push to main. Start the next one with "Read PROGRESS.md and continue from what's next." Open https://github.com/your-username/your-repo. The README describes your subject, CLAUDE.md holds your rules, and the newest commit on main shows your name, not Claude's.
Second example: a minisite with a sidebar

Use startup-india-guide when your subject needs several pages that people browse and search, not one story: a directory, a handbook, a resource guide or a program catalog. The Florida ecosystem map and this guide were both built from it. The example is a resource guide for new founders in your city.

Fork fritzhand/startup-india-guide into my account, with only the main branch, and name the fork your-repo. If you can't choose the fork's name, stop and tell me. Don't fork it under another name. If the agent can't, use the Fork button on https://github.com/fritzhand/startup-india-guide, as in step 1 above.

Claude in the app can't change that folder, because GitHub refuses the push, and on the VS Code path the agent may not be able to either. So delete it yourself on GitHub. On your fork, open the .github folder, then workflows. Click the three-dot menu (…) at the top right, then Delete directory. Click Commit changes.
Start a session and clean out the original owner's things

Start a session in your repo and send the rules, as in step 2 above. Then say: Pull the latest changes from GitHub first. In site.config.json, set siteName to "Founder Guide: My City", siteBase to https://your-username.github.io/your-repo/, pathPrefix to /your-repo/ and repo to https://github.com/your-username/your-repo, and delete analyticsId. Delete scripts/fetch-india-news.py; it feeds a daily news bot I don't need. Replace the author footer in build.mjs with my name, Your Name, and delete site/jeremy.png. Research the programs, funders, coworking spaces and events for new founders in my city. Give a working link for every entry, write everything to research/notes.md and mark anything you couldn't verify as TBD. Never invent a name, number, date or link. Then read build.mjs, site.config.json and the data folder, and plan how to turn this site into a resource guide for new founders in my city: which pages to keep, rename or delete, and which data file each page reads. Keep the sidebar, the search and the page layout. Don't change the site until I say go. Read what comes back, then say "Go ahead with the plan, using only research/notes.md." This engine was written for India, so the rewrite can take a few sessions. End each one with the PROGRESS.md prompt above.

Search the whole repo, ignoring capitals, for leftover words from the original that a visitor would see: India, scheme and fritzhand. Don't rename code names or file names the build reads. Keep the LICENSE file as it is, and fix every other word a visitor or reader would see, including README.md. Run node build.mjs until it finishes without errors, then commit and push to main. Then turn on GitHub Pages from main and /docs. Other subjects that fit this starter: a handbook for your club, a catalog of the programs your school offers, a directory of local nonprofits.

The site looks broken after a change Describe what you see and let the agent compare it with the original: The page now describe what looks wrong. Compare my repo with fritzhand/history-of-tampa, find what broke and fix it. Or go back one step: "Revert the last commit and push to main." A number or source looks made up Check every figure in js/data.js against research/notes.md. Remove anything that has no working source link, or mark it TBD. List what you changed. The push fails with a message about "workflow" GitHub refused a change to the .github/workflows folder. If you meant to delete that folder, do it yourself on GitHub, as in the second example. Then say: GitHub refused my push because it changes the .github/workflows folder. Pull the latest changes from GitHub, redo my unpushed work as one new commit that leaves that folder exactly as it is on GitHub, then commit and push to main. What the agent runs for you # Fork and clone, with only the main branch (GitHub CLI) gh repo fork fritzhand/history-of-tampa --clone --default-branch-only --fork-name your-repo # Find leftover words from the original grep -rniE "tampa|ybor|fritzhand" --exclude-dir=.git . # The starter's own data check (needs Node) node tools/validate-data.mjs # Save and publish git add . git commit -m "Rewrite the site for St. Petersburg" git push origin main

d: GitHub Pages turns the files on your main branch into a public website. You switch it on once. After that, every push to main updates your site.
s: Before you start, check two things: Your repo is public. On a free GitHub account, Pages works only from public repos. Its name is lowercase. Web addresses are case-sensitive, so a name with capitals is easy to mistype and gets a 404. Pages publishes one branch and one folder of your repo. Your site's address is built from your username and your repo name.

Pick the folder that holds your site's index.html: / (root) for history-of-tampa, or /docs for startup-india-guide. This is a setting on GitHub's website, and the app can't switch it for you. It takes a minute in any browser, including your phone's. Open https://github.com/your-username/your-repo/settings/pages. Or open your repo, click Settings (inside the More menu if you can't see it), then Pages in the left sidebar. Under Build and deployment, set Source to Deploy from a branch. Under Branch, choose main, then the folder: / (root) or /docs. Click Save. The agent does it with the GitHub CLI you signed in to in Git, Node & GitHub CLI. Turn on GitHub Pages for your-username/your-repo from the main branch, root folder (or /docs if the site lives in docs/), using the GitHub CLI, then tell me the URL. Switch to the App path tab above and follow its four steps. They work in any browser.

The first publish can take up to 10 minutes. To watch it, open your repo's Actions tab: a run called pages build and deployment appears, and a green check means it's done. I get a 404 page Wait the full 10 minutes, then reload. In Settings → Pages, check the branch is main and the folder is the one that holds index.html. It says git, node or gh is "not recognized" or "not found", but I just installed it Close every VS Code window and open VS Code again. It only finds new tools when it starts. On Windows, restart the computer if that doesn't help. Then say: Show me the versions of git, node and gh, and confirm gh is logged in. VS Code says Restricted Mode, or the agent doesn't work in my folder Do this yourself, because agents are turned off until you trust the folder. Open the Command Palette (Ctrl + Shift + P, or Cmd + Shift + P on Mac), run Workspaces: Manage Workspace Trust and trust the folder. Trust only folders you made or cloned from someone you trust. Codex needs ChatGPT Plus or higher. Check your plan, then sign in again.

The push was rejected Pull first, then push again. Don't force-push. Someone, maybe you on another device, pushed first. A force-push would overwrite their changes on GitHub. Git asks for my password or a token when it pushes Git is asking me for a password to push. Check whether the GitHub CLI is logged in and set up to sign Git in to GitHub, and tell me exactly what I need to do. Don't type your GitHub password there. GitHub no longer accepts passwords for Git, and you don't need a token. Run gh auth login yourself and say yes when it offers to use your GitHub login for Git, as shown in Git, Node & GitHub CLI. On Windows, Git for Windows can also sign you in through your browser. My commits say "Claude" instead of my name For this repo, set git user.name to "Your Name" and user.email to "your-noreply-email", and commit as me from now on. Then put the rule in CLAUDE.md so the next session follows it too. Older commits keep their author. See Commit as yourself. My commits don't show on my GitHub profile Show me the author name, email and branch of my last 5 commits. A commit counts only if its email is your noreply address or another email on your account, the repo isn't a fork, and the commit is on main. Then allow up to 24 hours. Commits in a fork never count, so make a fresh copy instead: Clone, fork or copy. I committed a password, key or token First, on the site that issued it, change the password, or cancel the key and make a new one. Deleting the file isn't enough, because the history keeps it. Then: Remove the file with the secret from the repo and add it to .gitignore so it can't be committed again. Then commit and push to main. The agent changed the wrong repo Undo your changes in the other repo. Work only in your-username/your-repo. Treat the other repos as read-only reference. Then add the "never invent facts" rule to your CLAUDE.md, as in the Prompt cheat sheet. The agent is going in circles Stop it. Start a new session (in VS Code, a new conversation), so the confusion doesn't carry over. Give it one clear goal and the exact error: Here's what I want: what done looks like. Here's the exact error: paste the exact error. Tell me what you think is wrong and your plan. Don't change anything until I say go. Still stuck? Then wait for the green check in your repo's Actions tab, up to 10 minutes, and open the address in a private or incognito window, which skips the copy your browser saved. I get a 404 page My site at https://your-username.github.io/your-repo/ shows a 404. Check that index.html, in lowercase, is in the folder GitHub Pages publishes from on main, tell me which branch and folder Pages should use, and fix anything in the repo. d: The words this guide uses, in plain English. Each one links to the page where you'll use it.
s: Agent An AI program that works on your files for you: it reads them, edits them and runs commands, then tells you what it did. In this guide the agent is Claude Code or Codex. See The big picture. Claude Code Anthropic's coding agent. You can use it in the Claude app, in a browser, on your phone or on your desktop, or as an extension inside VS Code. It needs a paid Claude plan. See App or VS Code? Codex OpenAI's coding agent. This guide uses its VS Code extension, which needs ChatGPT Plus or higher. See VS Code + your agent. Prompt What you type or say to the agent. A good one says what you want, where, and what done looks like. See How to talk to the agent. Session One conversation with the agent. A new session doesn't carry over your earlier conversations, so standing rules go in CLAUDE.md. See The big picture. Dictation Speaking instead of typing. Your phone, Mac or Windows computer turns what you say into text in the message box. See How to talk to the agent. Placeholder A highlighted part of a prompt, like your-username, that stands for your own details. Save your details in this guide and it fills them in for you. See Create your GitHub account. CLAUDE.md A plain text file at the root, or top folder, of your repo that holds standing rules, such as who to commit as. Claude reads it at the start of every session. Codex reads a file called AGENTS.md instead. See Prompt cheat sheet. Claude GitHub App A GitHub add-on that gives Claude in the app access to the repos you choose. Claude needs it to work in a private repo. See Claude Code in the app.

GitHub A website that stores your repos and their history, and can publish them as websites. A free account is all you need. See Create your GitHub account. Git The tool that records every saved version of your files and sends them to GitHub. The agent runs it for you. See Git, Node & GitHub CLI. Repository (repo) Your project's folder on GitHub, plus the history of every saved change. Your site lives in one repo. See Repos: public or private. Public and private Who can see a repo. Anyone can see a public repo, including its history. Only you and people you invite can see a private one. On a free account, GitHub Pages works only from public repos. README The file GitHub shows on a repo's front page, usually README.md. It says what the repo is. Commit A save point for the whole project, with a short note that says what changed. You can go back to any commit. See Commit & push. Author The name and email recorded on each commit. It decides who gets the credit on GitHub. See Commit as yourself. Noreply email A private address GitHub gives you, ending in @users.noreply.github.com. Use it as your commit email: it credits you without putting your real email in public. See Create your GitHub account. Push Sends your commits up to GitHub. Until you push, they exist only in the working copy. A force-push overwrites what's on GitHub, so avoid it. See Commit & push. Pull Brings changes down from GitHub into your working copy, such as edits you made on another device. See Commit & push. Clone A working copy of a repo, on your computer or in the cloud. It stays linked to the repo, so the agent can push changes back. See Clone, fork or copy. Working copy The copy of your repo that the agent edits: a folder on your computer on the VS Code path, or a fresh copy in the cloud on the app path. See The big picture. Fork Your own copy of someone else's repo, on GitHub, still linked to the original. A fork of a public repo stays public, and commits in it don't count on your GitHub profile. See Clone, fork or copy. Template A repo set up so that its Use this template button makes you a fresh repo, with no link back. The starters in this guide aren't set up as templates, so you fork them or make a fresh copy. See Clone, fork or copy. Branch A parallel line of work in the same repo. Changes on a branch don't touch the main line until they're merged. See The main branch. main The main branch of your repo. GitHub Pages publishes your site from it, so your site changes only when main changes. In the app, Claude works on its own claude/… branch first. See The main branch. Pull request (PR) A request to merge the changes on one branch into another. GitHub shows the changes so you can look before you click Merge pull request. See The main branch. Merge Combining the changes from one branch into another, such as a claude/… branch into main. See The main branch. Merge conflict Two changes touched the same lines, and Git can't tell which to keep. Ask the agent to explain it before you choose. See Commit & push. Revert Undoing a commit by adding a new commit that reverses it, so the record stays. See Commit & push.

VS Code A free code editor from Microsoft. On the VS Code path, your agent runs inside it. See VS Code + your agent. Extension An add-on that gives VS Code a new feature. The Claude Code and Codex extensions put the agent in a panel inside VS Code. See VS Code + your agent. Terminal A window where you type commands instead of clicking. In VS Code, open it with View → Terminal. You'll rarely need it, because the agent runs commands for you. Trusted folder (Workspace Trust) VS Code asks whether you trust the authors of the files in a folder. Say no, and it opens the folder in Restricted Mode, with AI agents and the terminal turned off. Trust only folders you made or cloned from someone you trust. See Trusted folders. GitHub CLI (gh) A GitHub tool the agent runs to do GitHub chores for you, such as creating or forking a repo and turning on GitHub Pages. You sign it in once with gh auth login. See Git, Node & GitHub CLI. Node.js A free program that runs JavaScript on your computer. Some starters need it for their build step. The agents themselves don't. See Git, Node & GitHub CLI. Execution policy The Windows PowerShell setting that decides whether scripts may run. Its starting value blocks the scripts Node's tools use. See Windows: allow scripts.

GitHub Pages GitHub's free website hosting. It publishes one branch and one folder of your repo at https://your-username.github.io/your-repo/. See Turn on GitHub Pages. index.html The page a site opens with. GitHub Pages needs it named in lowercase, in the folder it publishes from. See Turn on GitHub Pages. Build step A command that turns a site's source files into its finished pages, such as node build.mjs. history-of-tampa has none. startup-india-guide builds its pages into a docs folder. See Pick a starter. Actions tab The tab on your repo where GitHub lists its automatic jobs. Each time your site publishes, a run called pages build and deployment appears there, and a green check means it's done. See Turn on GitHub Pages.

d: Who made this guide, why, and how it's built. It's a GitHub repo published with GitHub Pages, the same way your site will be.
s: Jeremy Fritzhand, fritzhand on GitHub. He also made the starter sites the guide points to.

It's the shortest path from no GitHub account to a published website, made by telling an AI agent what you want. It teaches only what you need for that one goal. There are no servers, databases or frameworks here. You type or dictate, and the agent does the work.

This site is itself a repo, fritzhand/quickstart, published with GitHub Pages from main and the /docs folder. It was made with Claude Code, by the same steps the guide teaches. Each page is one HTML file in the content folder. content/nav.json sets the sidebar and the page order. node build.mjs turns them into the finished site in docs. It needs Node.js and nothing else. Want a guide like this one about your own topic? Fork it: Fork fritzhand/quickstart into my account and name the fork your-repo. Then point it at your own address: Work only in your-username/your-repo. Treat the other repos as read-only reference. In site.config.json, set siteName to "My Guide", siteBase to https://your-username.github.io/your-repo/, pathPrefix to /your-repo/ and repo to https://github.com/your-username/your-repo, and set the author to my name, Your Name, with https://github.com/your-username. Run node build.mjs until it finishes without errors, then commit and push to main. Its CLAUDE.md explains the page format to the agent, and after each change the agent rebuilds the docs folder. Publish from main and /docs, as in Turn on GitHub Pages.
